parts.title: Early Bird Special: Counting How Often Tiger Sharks Eat Young Albatrosses at Kure Atoll
parts.abstract:
ABSTRACT

In the ocean, a predator and its prey can be linked by a regular, seasonal burst of food. Yet in the sea, we still have very little direct evidence of how three things change over time: when predators are around, when prey are available, and how often the predators actually catch them.

Every year, young albatrosses (Laysan albatross, Phoebastria immutabilis, and black-footed albatross, P. nigripes) leave their breeding colonies to learn to fly. We call these young birds fledglings. At these colonies, tiger sharks (Galeocerdo cuvier) gather again and again at the same time of year. Until now, though, nobody had measured when these meetings happen or how they unfold.

We watched and counted these meetings directly for a whole fledging season at Kure Atoll, in the Northwestern Hawaiian Islands. We looked at how four things changed over time: how often we saw sharks at the surface, how many fledglings there were, what in the environment might be driving these patterns, how often the sharks actually caught birds, and how the risk of being eaten changed through the season.

We saw the most tiger sharks 28 days before the number of fledglings was highest. This suggests that the sharks and the birds are out of step in time. The sharks seem to prefer the early stage, when fledglings are most vulnerable, rather than the time when there are the most birds.

Weather and other environmental conditions had only weak and uncertain effects on both shark sightings and fledgling numbers. The timing of the season was the main thing shaping the patterns we saw.

When a shark and a fledgling met, the shark rarely caught the bird on the first try. But once a meeting had started, the shark was very likely to end up eating the bird. This shows that repeated attack attempts play a big part in whether a shark succeeds.

The risk of being eaten was highest early in the fledging season. This was mainly because that is when sharks and vulnerable fledglings were in the water at the same time, not because the sharks' behavior or the number of birds changed.

More broadly, our findings suggest that how predators respond to a predictable burst of prey may depend on how vulnerable that prey is. This points to a key way that predator behavior connects to the patterns of who eats whom in nature.

Keywords: how often predators and prey meet, seasonal timing of events, predator–prey relationships, short bursts of food, shark–seabird relationships
parts.introduction_first: In the ocean, a predator and its prey can be linked by a regular, seasonal burst of food (Davoren et al. 2024). Even so, in many ocean places we still know little about how three things change over time: when predators are around, when prey are available, and how often the predators actually catch them (Lovell et al. 2024). Because of this, scientists often learn about these relationships from indirect clues or from computer models that look at very large areas. Those approaches may miss the fine detail of how things change from hour to hour (Huse and Fiksen 2010), or they may not fully answer how things change across a whole seasonal event.
parts.introduction_rest:
Seabird breeding colonies give us a special chance to study these questions. At a colony, many young birds leave the nest at almost the same time (Rice and Kenyon 1962). This creates short, predictable bursts of young, inexperienced prey entering the ocean (Meyer et al. 2009, 2010). At Kure Atoll, in the Northwestern Hawaiian Islands, young Laysan albatrosses (Phoebastria immutabilis) and black-footed albatrosses (P. nigripes) all enter the water within a narrow window of time. This may put them at risk of being eaten by tiger sharks (Galeocerdo cuvier). Tiger sharks are top predators that roam over huge areas, but they are known to gather in places where food is available at predictable times (Meyer et al. 2009, 2010; Blandino et al. 2025).

When fledglings first move from land to sea, they are especially easy to catch. Before they leave, they strengthen their wings by flapping again and again and by making short test flights. Often they land in the lagoon, the shallow water inside the ring of coral, and then fly back to shore (Rice and Kenyon 1962). Birds that leave the colony before they can fly well may end up stranded on the water. There they cannot take off properly, they get soaked and heavy, or they are eaten or starve (Rice and Kenyon 1962). Wind matters too. It gives fledglings the lift they need to fly, but strong winds can sometimes cause problems (VanderWerf et al. 2019). Together, how well a fledgling can fly and the conditions around it may affect how long it spends in the water, and so how long it is exposed to predators.

Still, we do not know how four things line up in time during these events: when predators are present, when prey are available, how often the predators catch them, and what the environment is like. For example, other scientists have suggested that ocean conditions such as temperature, tides and currents may shape how predators and prey interact. But these non-living conditions change, which makes it hard to tell what is really going on (Schalff et al. 2014). Tiger sharks and albatross fledglings meet at the same time of year, and this overlap is predictable. That gives us a rare chance to study how these three species, all of them near-threatened, interact. In this study, we measured the timing of tiger shark sightings and the number of fledglings, along with how often the sharks caught birds, during one fledging season at Kure Atoll. We also looked at which local conditions in the environment might be linked to how often the sharks caught birds.

We watched and counted tiger sharks and fledgling albatrosses directly, across the whole fledging season. We had four goals: (1) to see how tiger shark sightings relate to the number of fledglings and to what the fledglings were doing, (2) to find out how the environment affects tiger shark sightings and the number of fledglings, (3) to measure how often the sharks caught birds, and (4) to look for patterns in how often the sharks caught birds through the season. We expected three things. First, we expected tiger shark sightings to peak when the number of fledglings was highest, because that is when predators and prey would be in the water together most often. Second, we expected wind to affect how many chances fledglings had to fly and how long they spent in the water. Third, we expected higher tides to bring more tiger shark sightings, because the water is shallow there, and higher tides would make it easier for these large animals to reach the birds.
parts.methods:
## 2. Materials and Methods

### 2.1. Ethics Statement

This research was approved and carried out under two permits: Papahānaumokuākea Marine National Monument Conservation and Management Permit #PMNM‐2024‐001 and James Cook University Animal Ethics Permit #26A‐0015.

### 2.2. Where We Did the Study

Kure Atoll (28°25′ N, 178°20′ W) sits at the far end of the chain of the Northwestern Hawaiian Islands. It lies inside the Papahānaumokuākea Marine National Monument, about 1200 km from Honolulu, Hawaii (Figure 1). An atoll is a ring of coral reef around a lagoon. Kure's lagoon is circular and 9.6 km wide. It is shaped by the reef around it, which rises more than 100 m from the ocean floor. The reef has a "groove and spur" shape, with long, low ridges (spurs) running between deeper channels (grooves).

Green Island, which covers 85 hectares, lies inside the lagoon. The lagoon is between 0 and 10 m deep, and most of it is less than 5 m deep (Friedlander et al. 2009).

FIGURE 1

Map of the survey site. The red dot in the small inset map shows where Kure Atoll sits among the Northwestern Hawaiian Islands. The yellow dot marks the raised spot where we watched the lagoon. The shaded blue shape shows the area we could see from there. The shape of the reef comes from habitat maps of the seafloor made by the NOAA Pacific Islands Benthic Habitat Mapping Center (PBHMC) for Kure Atoll, Northwestern Hawaiian Islands (NOAA NCCOS 2003).

### 2.3. How We Collected the Data

We counted predators and prey, and watched how they met, through daily surveys by eye. We did this from 21 May 2024 to 20 September 2024, which was 122 days. That covered the whole 2024 fledging season for Laysan and black-footed albatrosses, plus 2 weeks after we last saw a fledgling.

We surveyed three times a day: in the morning, at midday and in the evening. Surveys lasted anywhere from 11 to 157 minutes. On average they lasted 55 minutes, and the middle value (the median) was 60 minutes. We watched from a raised spot off the tip of Green Island's pier, looking over the lagoon. On average it was 6.6 m above the water, though its height changed with the tide. Surveying at the same times every day gave us even coverage across the whole fledging season. It also let us look for seasonal patterns in when we saw tiger sharks and fledglings, and in how the sharks and birds met.

Each survey began with us recording conditions at the watching spot. We then scanned the lagoon in a set order, helped by Celestron Nature DX binoculars (Torrance, California, USA). We counted and recorded every tiger shark and fledgling we could see in the survey area. For albatrosses, we counted fledglings in the water inside the survey area. Birds that stayed on land or the beach were not included.

Throughout each survey, we tracked new birds as they entered the area and followed the movements of birds we had already counted. This kept our counts consistent and stopped us from counting the same bird twice. The area we watched covered about 24% (17.2 km²) of the lagoon. The lagoon is circular and 9.6 km wide (Friedlander et al. 2009), so its total area is about 72 km² (Figure 1).

At the start of each survey, we measured conditions that might affect shark counts, fledgling numbers and how the two met (Table 1). We used a Kestrel 4000 Pocket Weather Tracker to measure air temperature, air pressure, wind speed and wind direction. We judged the direction of waves and tides by eye, using a compass. To measure tide height, we compared the water against a marked reference point at the seaward edge of the pier. Tide heights ranged from 69 to 127 cm, with an average of 96 cm and a median of 97 cm.

We called the water either clear or murky. We did this by checking whether we could see the place where the reef break meets the surf, from the top of the watching spot. We judged cloud cover and rain using United States Air Force Manual 15–111: Surface Weather Observations (U.S. Department of the Air Force 2020).

TABLE 1

Conditions we recorded at the start of each survey, and why we thought each might help predict tiger shark sightings and fledgling counts.

| Variable | Unit of measure | Variable type | Why we included it |
|---|---|---|---|
| Air temperature | Degrees Celsius | Continuous | Affects heat stress in fledglings (Mason et al. 2024) |
| Air pressure | Inches of mercury (inHg) | Continuous | A clue to changing weather systems (Schalff et al. 2014; Udyawer et al. 2013) |
| Wind speed | Knots (nearest whole knot) | Continuous | Affects surface conditions and sea state, which affect where prey are and how birds fly (Udyawer et al. 2013; Weltz et al. 2013) |
| Wind direction | Compass direction | Categorical | Affects chances for birds to fly, and drives the direction of currents (Weltz et al. 2013) |
| Wave direction | Compass direction | Categorical | Affects where floating prey end up |
| Tide height | Centimeters (nearest whole cm) | Continuous | Affects how easily animals can reach their habitat (Schalff et al. 2014) |
| Cloud cover | Percentage | Continuous | Affects light levels, shark activity and how easily observers can see (Schalff et al. 2014) |
| Rain intensity | Rain intensity class | Categorical | Affects how well we can see, how disturbed the surface is, and how easily observers can see |
| Water clarity | Water clarity class, judged by eye | Categorical | Affects how well predators, prey and observers can see |

Note: Each variable is listed with its units, its type of data, and the reason we included it in our later analyses. "Continuous" means a number that can take any value. "Categorical" means a group, such as a compass direction.

We recorded every shark sighting, including which species it was. At the start of each survey, we counted the Laysan and black-footed albatross fledglings. To avoid counting the same bird twice, we noted when new birds entered the lagoon and followed the movements of birds we had already counted. This gave us the largest number of different birds seen during each survey, which we call MaxIND (Sherman et al. 2018). We recorded every meeting between a shark and an albatross. For each meeting, we noted whether the shark caught the bird, whether it failed, and how many times it bit.

### 2.4. Preparing the Data

Before building our statistical models, we explored and cleaned the data. We dealt with three issues: conditions that rose and fell together, units that needed to match, and surveys that lasted different lengths of time.

First, we checked whether any conditions were so closely linked that they carried almost the same information. This problem is called collinearity. We looked at it with scatterplot matrices, which are grids of graphs showing every pair of conditions, using the car package (Fox and Weisberg 2019). We measured how closely two conditions moved together with a number called r. When r was 0.7 or more, or −0.7 or less, we treated the two as too closely linked and did not use both in the analysis (Dormann et al. 2013). When we had to choose between two conditions that carried the same information, we picked the one that measured the condition directly. For example, we used wind speed rather than the Beaufort wind scale, and the day of the year (Julian day) rather than the survey date.

Next, we put all conditions on the same scale and converted measurements from imperial units to SI (metric) units. We turned survey dates into the day of the year, so that sampling was lined up evenly across the whole study. We turned survey length from minutes into hours as a decimal. We then took the logarithm of survey length. This let us adjust for the fact that some surveys were longer than others. We ran every model only on complete records, leaving out any record with a missing value.

### 2.5. How We Analyzed the Data

We analyzed the data in four stages, one for each aim of the study. Each stage used a different kind of model, and the stages built on one another (Table 2).

First, we used Bayesian generalized additive mixed models (GAMMs) to describe how tiger shark sightings and fledgling counts changed through the season. Second, we used boosted regression tree (BRT) models to find which conditions were linked to the seasonal patterns we saw. We then used the conditions that mattered most in the BRT models to build Bayesian generalized linear mixed models (GLMMs). These looked at the effects of the key conditions while taking into account how the data were grouped in time. Finally, we used simple summaries and Bayesian analyses to measure how often sharks caught birds and how the risk of being eaten changed through the season.

TABLE 2

Overview of the analysis plan.

| Aim | Question about nature | Statistical approach |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | When in the fledging season are tiger shark sightings and fledglings most common? | GAMMs |
| 2 | Which conditions best explain shark sightings and prey numbers? | Gradient boosted regression trees, followed by GLMMs |
| 3 | How often do sharks try to catch birds, and how often do they succeed? | Simple summaries |
| 4 | When is the overall risk of a strike greatest? | Hierarchical ecological process model |

Note: Four questions about nature, asked one after another, each answered with a different kind of model.

Table 3 shows the exact model we used for each aim. For each one, it lists what we were trying to explain, the kind of data we assumed, the conditions we used, and the purpose of the analysis. Sections 2.5.1 and 2.5.4 describe each approach in detail, including how we checked that the models fitted well.

TABLE 3

The analysis plan and model details for each aim.

| Analysis | What we tried to explain | Data type assumed | Model structure & formula | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Seasonal timing (Aim 1) | Tiger shark sightings | Zero-inflated Poisson (link = "log", link_zi = "logit") | Julian day + survey effort offset + random intercept for survey period time of day: tiger_sharks ~ s(julian_day) + offset(log(survey_length)) + (1|time_of_day) | Estimate how shark sightings change through the season, allowing for curved patterns, and account for differences in survey effort and for repeated daily sampling (AM, MIDDAY, PM) |
| | Fledgling counts | Negative binomial (link = "log") | Julian day + survey effort offset + random intercept for survey period time of day: chicks ~ s(julian_day) + offset(log(survey_length)) + (1|time_of_day) | Same as for tiger sharks, but for fledgling numbers |
| Conditions that drive the patterns (Aim 2) | Tiger shark sightings | Poisson (link = "log") | Atmospheric pressure + wind direction + survey effort offset + random intercepts for survey period and Julian day: tiger_sharks ~ pressure_inhg_c + wind_direction + offset(log(survey_hours)) + (1 | time_of_day) + (1 | julian_day) | Measure how shark sightings relate to the conditions picked out by the BRT analyses |
| | Fledgling counts | Zero-inflated Poisson (link = "log", link_zi = "logit") | Tide height + wind direction + survey effort offset + random intercepts for survey period and Julian day: chicks ~ tide_cm_c, + wind_direction + offset(log(survey_hours)) + (1 | time_of_day) + (1 | julian_day) | Measure how fledgling counts relate to the conditions picked out by the BRT analyses |
| Measuring how often sharks catch birds (Aim 3) | Shark success | — | Simple summaries, not formally analyzed | Summarize how often sharks and birds met and what happened |
| Where sharks are (Aim 4) | Shark sightings, present or absent | Bernoulli (link = "logit") | Standardized Julian day + standardized log survey duration + random intercept for survey period time of day | Estimate how the chance of seeing tiger sharks changes through the season, allowing for curved patterns |
| Where prey are (Aim 4) | Fledgling presence, present or absent | Bernoulli (link = "logit") | Standardized Julian day + standardized log survey duration + random intercept for survey period time of day | Estimate how the chance of fledglings being present changes through the season, allowing for curved patterns |
| Chance of a strike once both are present (Aim 4) | Successful strike | Binomial (link = "complementary log–log") | Standardized Julian day + standardized log survey duration + random intercept for survey period time of day | Estimate the chance of a successful strike, given that a shark and a fledgling were seen together |
| Overall chance of a strike (Aim 4) | Overall chance of a strike, worked out from the model | — | Worked out by multiplying the predictions from the shark presence, fledgling presence and strike models | Estimate the overall chance of a strike during a survey |

Note: The model structures are simplified to make them easier to read. A "smooth" term (for example, "s(julian_day)") is a flexible curve that can bend to follow the data, with a penalty that stops it from becoming too wiggly. Before analysis, we centered each condition measured as a number by subtracting its average. These are marked with "_c" in the formulas. Survey effort was included either as a log-transformed offset (for count models) or as a standardized, log-transformed extra factor (for yes-or-no models). Random intercepts allowed for repeated observations within the same survey period, and where shown, within the same day of the year. Table 5 lists the shared settings we used to fit the Bayesian models.

We fitted all Bayesian models with the brms package (Bürkner 2017), using the CmdStan engine (Stan Development Team 2023). Bayesian models start from "priors", which are starting assumptions about what values are reasonable. We used weakly informative priors, based on the median and the median absolute deviation of each thing we were trying to explain. The median is the middle value, and the median absolute deviation measures how spread out the values are. These priors kept the estimates from becoming unrealistic while still letting the data shape the relationships in nature (Lemoine 2019).

We checked how well the models worked in several ways. We compared the data the models predicted before and after seeing the real data, to see whether those predictions matched the real patterns (Gelman et al. 2020; McElreath 2020). We also checked that the models had settled on a stable answer, a step called convergence. For this we used trace plots, effective sample sizes and R^ checks (Vehtari et al. 2021). We checked the leftover differences between the models and the data, called residuals, with the DHARMa package (Hartig 2024). All models mixed well and settled on a stable answer (R^ < 1.01), with enough effective samples.

#### 2.5.1. Seasonal Timing of Tiger Shark Sightings and Fledgling Counts (Aim 1)

To describe the seasonal timing of tiger shark sightings and fledgling numbers, we fitted GAMMs to the survey data in R (R Core Team 2025). These models aimed to estimate when the seasonal patterns happened and what shape they had. They did not aim to find what in the environment caused the changes. We looked at environmental conditions separately in Aim 2.

We modeled tiger shark sightings and fledgling numbers separately against the day of the year. We included the day of the year as a smooth curve, so the models could follow a trend that bends rather than a straight line (Table 3). We included survey effort, in hours as a decimal, as a log-offset. This allowed for the way longer or shorter surveys might affect the number of tiger sharks seen and the number of fledglings.

We included the time of day (AM, MIDDAY, PM) as a random effect. This allowed for steady differences between the three survey periods and for the fact that we sampled the same periods again and again within each day. To find the seasonal timing of the median prediction, we looked for the day of the year when the running total of the predicted numbers reached 50% of the season total. We also gave 95% credible intervals for this. A credible interval is the range in which the true value most likely lies, given the data and the model.

#### 2.5.2. Environmental Conditions That Drive Seasonal Patterns (Aim 2)

We used gradient boosted regression tree (BRT) models to explore which conditions drove tiger shark sightings and fledgling numbers, one at a time (De'ath 2007; Elith et al. 2008; Hastie et al. 2009). A BRT builds many simple decision trees, one after another. Each new tree fixes mistakes left by the ones before it, so the trees "boost" one another.

The conditions we recorded during each survey were air temperature, air pressure, wind speed and direction, tide height, wave direction, cloud cover, rain intensity and water clarity (Table 1). We also recorded the time of day and the time of season (day of the year). We included a log-transformed survey length as an offset to allow for differences in how much we sampled. We did not measure water temperature in this study because the equipment was not available, though we recognize that having these data would be ideal.

At French Frigate Shoals, time of day is known to be an important driver of how many sharks are around when albatross fledglings are present (Blandino et al. 2025). Here, we allowed for an effect of time of day while testing for effects of other conditions, such as wind direction, wind speed and air temperature. We ran all BRT analyses in R using the gbm package (Ridgeway and GBM Developers 2026).

We built separate Poisson models for tiger shark counts and for fledgling numbers. A Poisson model is a standard choice for counts. Each model used the environmental conditions, with survey effort as an offset. We tuned the model settings separately for each model (Table 4). These settings included the learning rate, the interaction depth, the minimum number of observations per node, and the number of trees. We chose the number of trees using threefold cross-validation (Elith et al. 2008). In cross-validation, the data are split into three parts. The model learns from two parts and is tested on the third, and this is repeated so that each part gets a turn.

The final settings gave 943 trees for the tiger shark model and 1472 trees for the fledgling model. We then worked out the confidence intervals and relative influence of each condition, using the best number of trees. We did this by bootstrapping 1000 times, which means resampling the data at random 1000 times and seeing how much the results changed. We treated a condition as having a significant relative influence if it passed a threshold calculated as 100/12 variables.

TABLE 4

Settings for the gradient boosted regression tree (BRT) models used to find conditions linked to tiger shark counts and fledgling counts.

| Parameter | Tiger shark model | Fledgling model |
|---|---|---|
| Distribution (loss function) | Poisson | Poisson |
| Learning rate | 0.0002 | 0.01 |
| Tree complexity | 10,000 | 10,000 |
| Interaction depth | 2 | 3 |
| Bag fraction | 0.5 | 0.5 |
| n.trees | 943 | 1472 |
| Train fraction | 1 | 1 |
| n.minobsinnode | 10 | 5 |
| Cross-validation folds | 3 | 3 |
| Model structure | gbm(tiger_sharks ~ julian_day + wind_direction + tide_cm + temp_c + pressure_inhg + wind_knots + cloud_cover + precipitation + wave_direction + tide_direction + water_clarity + time_of_day + offset(log(survey_hours)) | gbm(chicks ~ julian_day + wind_direction + tide_cm + temp_c + pressure_inhg + wind_knots + cloud_cover + precipitation + wave_direction + tide_direction + water_clarity + time_of_day + offset(log(survey_hours)) |

Note: We fitted separate models for tiger sharks and albatross fledglings. Both used environmental conditions, survey length as an effort offset, and the day of the year to account for seasonal change. Distribution = the type of data assumed for fitting; Learning rate = how much each tree adds to the overall model; Tree complexity = the largest number of trees tried while fitting; Interaction depth = the most conditions allowed to work together in a tree; Bag fraction = the share of the data picked at random to build each tree; n.trees = the number of trees chosen by cross-validation; Train fraction = the share of observations used to fit the model; n.minobsinnode = the smallest number of observations allowed in the end points of a tree; Cross-validation folds = the number of parts the data were split into to test predictions; Code = the model formula used.

Before building the GLMMs, we looked at how the conditions picked out as important in the BRT analyses changed over time (Figure 2). Several of them rose and fell in cycles through the day of the year, even though they were not statistically collinear. We kept the top-ranked BRT conditions for the GLMM analysis. We recognize, though, that these cycles may make it harder to tell apart the effects of the separate conditions.

FIGURE 2

Environmental conditions recorded during tiger shark surveys across the study season. (A) Wind rose showing how many surveys took place in each wind direction and wind speed (knots). Wind direction changed throughout the season, but winds from the east were the most common, making up about 42% of surveys. (B) Air pressure (inHg) by day of the year, (C) tide height (cm) by day of the year, and (D) air temperature (°C) by day of the year. In panels B–D, green lines join the observations in order, to show the cycles in the conditions over time.

Based on the BRT analysis, we then tested the top-ranked condition for each thing we were trying to explain, using Bayesian GLMMs. We modeled tiger shark sightings against air pressure and wind direction. We modeled fledgling numbers against wind direction and tide height. The day of the year had a high relative influence on both shark counts and fledgling numbers. Even so, we did not include it as a fixed effect in the GLMMs. A fixed effect is a condition whose effect the model estimates directly. We left it out because we had already tested its relationship with shark counts and fledgling numbers directly in the seasonal analyses (Aim 1).

Instead, we included the day of the year and the time of day as random effects. This took into account how the data were grouped, and the fact that observations from repeated surveys are not independent of one another (Harrison 2014; Wood 2017). These terms let the models allow for differences between survey dates and between the daily survey periods, while reducing the variation the models could not explain. So we modeled both tiger shark sightings and fledgling numbers against only two conditions. This kept the models from overfitting, which means fitting the quirks of one particular dataset too closely, and made the results easier to interpret (Table 3).

We centered the conditions measured as numbers, tide height and air pressure. This made the model's starting value (the intercept) and its slopes easier to interpret, and helped the models converge. We modeled wind direction as a set of categories. We included survey effort as a log-offset to allow for differences in survey length. This assumed that the number of animals seen rises in proportion to how long we watched.

To make predictions, we created grids across the range of days of the year we observed. We kept survey length fixed at 60 minutes, the approximate median survey length, so that every prediction used the same amount of sampling. We fitted and checked the models using the standard steps described in Section 2.5.1 and Table 5.

TABLE 5

Shared settings we used to fit the Bayesian models.

| Setting | Study default | Exceptions | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| Software | brms (CmdStan) | — | brms package (Bürkner 2017) with cmdstand backend (Stan Development Team 2023) |
| Priors | Weakly informative | — | Prevent unrealistic estimates while capturing relationships in nature (Lemoine 2019) |
| Chains | 3 | Strike models: 4 | Number of independent Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) chains |
| Iterations | 8000 | Strike models: 10,000 | Total MCMC steps per chain |
| Warm-up | 1000 | Strike models: 2000 | Steps thrown away while the model adjusts before sampling |
| Thinning | 5 | Strike models: 7 | How often we kept a sample from the chain |
| adapt_delta | 0.95 | Strike models: 0.99 | Reduces errors in the sampling and makes it more efficient (Stan Development Team 2023) |
| max_treedepth | Default (10) | Strike models: 15 | Allows for more complex paths in the sampling |
| MCMC Diagnostics | R^, ESS, trace plots, posterior predictive checks | Applied to all models | R^ < 1.01 (Vehtari et al. 2021); bulk and tail effective sample size > 100 times the number of chains (Stan Development Team, n.d.); plots of how closely samples follow one another (Stan Development Team 2023); posterior predictive checks and residual checks with the DHARMa package (Hartig 2024) |

#### 2.5.3. How Often Sharks Caught Birds (Aim 3)

We estimated how often sharks caught birds using simple summaries. We saw only 26 meetings, which was too few to build a reliable statistical model of what predicted success. So we limited the analysis to summary measures of how often the sharks and birds met and what happened.

#### 2.5.4. Seasonal Change in How Often Sharks Caught Birds (Aim 4)

To model the chance of a shark catching a bird, we used a hierarchical ecological process model. This kind of model splits a process into several linked stages. We estimated the overall chance of a strike by modeling three things separately: where fledglings were, where sharks were, and the chance of a strike once both were present. We then combined them using the models' predictions (Kéry and Royle 2020; McElreath 2020).

In the first stage, we modeled the presence of prey (fledglings) and the presence of the predator (tiger sharks) separately, as yes-or-no outcomes depending on the day of the year. This measured how the chance of a meeting changed over time. In the second stage, we modeled the chance of a tiger shark striking a fledgling, given that the two were present together. In other words, both sharks and fledglings had to be seen as present.

For the shark and fledgling presence models, we used Bayesian binomial regression models with logit links. A binomial model handles yes-or-no outcomes, and a logit link turns the chance of a yes into a scale that can be added up. We included the centered day of the year as a smooth curve, so the models could follow trends that bend over time (Table 3). We included survey length as a log-transformed factor to allow for differences in how much we sampled. We included time of day as a random intercept to allow for repeated sampling within the same survey period.

For the behavior model, we modeled the chance of a strike with a Bayesian binomial regression using a complementary log–log link. This link lets us model the chance of an event that comes from an underlying rate (McCullagh and Nelder 1989). We modeled how strikes changed over time with a smooth curve of the centered day of the year. We included survey length as a log-transformed factor to allow for differences in how much we sampled, and fledgling presence as a fixed effect. We included time of day as a random intercept to allow for repeated sampling within the same survey period.

We fitted the strike model only to observations in which we saw both tiger sharks and fledglings. This kept the sharks' behavior separate from how often they met the birds. If we saw neither a predator nor a prey, no strike could happen, so we left those observations out of the behavior model. Instead, we handled them in the earlier stages, where we modeled the presence of prey and predator directly. Because of this, the overall chance of a strike during a survey comes close to zero whenever prey or predators are absent. This happens because the model multiplies its parts together.

We combined the predictions from each stage to estimate the overall chance of a strike during a survey:

P_strike = P_birds × P_sharks × P_strike(birds, sharks)

We made predictions for the whole population from 1000 posterior draws of each model, leaving out the random effects. A posterior draw is one possible set of values the model could take, given the data. We kept survey length fixed at its median value (60 minutes). We picked out the peaks in the chance of fledglings being present, the chance of sharks being present, and the overall chance of a strike. We did not do this for the strike model, because it showed no clear peak.

#### 2.5.5. Making the Figures and Maps

We made all figures with the ggplot2 package (Wickham 2016). We made the map of Kure Atoll in R (R Core Team 2025) using the packages sf, dplyr, ggspatial, cowplot and rnaturalearth. We also used map files of the reef's shape and of the seafloor habitats (kure_class_geog and kure_cover_geog) (NOAA National Centers for Coastal Ocean Science 2003).

The detailed habitat classes (HABCLASS) were grouped into broader habitat types that matter for how predators and prey meet. These were reef edge, reef, hardbottom, rubble, sand, deepwater and land. We treated the "surf" class as a stand-in for reef-edge habitat. We placed the watching spot and the estimated survey areas over the map by comparing our observation references with aerial maps. We did this using simple feature (sf) objects, which are map shapes tied to WGS84 geographic coordinates (EPSG:4326). We added a grid of latitude and longitude lines drawn by hand to give a sense of location. We made the inset map of the Hawaiian Islands using Natural Earth coastline data, cut to the area covering the Hawaiian Islands.

## 3. Results

### 3.1. How Much Watching We Did

From 21 May 2024 to 20 September 2024, we carried out 359 surveys on 122 days. Altogether we spent 325 hours and 57 minutes watching directly.

### 3.2. Seasonal Timing of Tiger Shark Sightings and Albatross Fledgling Counts (Aim 1)

In the lagoon, we saw and recorded 1564 fledglings of albatross species. That is 4.29% of all the nests counted across the whole island in December 2023 (Agreement on the Conservation of Albatrosses and Petrels 2024). It is also 7.29% of all the chicks counted across the island six months later, in June 2024 (N. Worcester, personal communication, June 20, 2026).

Across all our observations, we recorded 247 sharks. Of these, 43 were tiger sharks and 162 were Galapagos sharks. The other 42 were sharks large enough to rule out smaller species such as the Galapagos shark, but we could not say for certain that they were tiger sharks.

To follow how numbers changed through the season, we used a type of statistical model called a Bayesian generalized additive mixed model (GAMM). It fits a smooth curve through the data, so it can follow a rise and fall that is not a straight line. It also allows for the fact that some surveys were grouped together, for example by day or by time of day. We give dates as the day of the year, counting from 1 January. We also give a 95% credible interval (CrI) for each estimate. This is the range in which the true value most likely lies, given our data and model.

Fledgling numbers rose gradually from day 143 of the year. They reached their estimated peak on day 220 (7 August), 77 days after we first saw a fledgling in the lagoon (Figure 3B). The 95% credible interval for this peak was days 200 to 224. Fledgling numbers then fell quickly after the peak, and the last fledgling we saw in the lagoon was 30 days after the peak.

The smooth curve through the days of the year explained a moderate share of the ups and downs in fledgling numbers. We measured this with two numbers. The marginal R² (Rm) is the share of the variation explained by the main factors in the model, here the day of the year. The conditional R² (Rc) is the share explained by those main factors plus the extra variation linked to groups of surveys, such as surveys on the same day. For fledglings, Rm was 0.331 (95% CrI: 0.088–0.674) and Rc was 0.409 (95% CrI: 0.315–0.514). These results show that the timing of the season contributed a lot to the variation in fledgling numbers.

FIGURE 3

(A) Tiger shark sightings and (B) albatross fledgling numbers through the fledging season. (C) Both together, with tiger shark sightings in green (left axis) and fledgling numbers in blue (right axis, on a different scale). The lines show the model's estimated trends, and the shaded bands show the 95% credible intervals, which reflect how uncertain the estimates are. Red points mark estimated peak counts, and black points mark median counts. The horizontal bars show the uncertainty in when each of these happened.

Tiger shark sightings followed a balanced, bell-shaped pattern through the season. Sightings peaked on day 192 (95% CrI: days 182–200). The median, or middle, sighting was on day 191 (10 July; 95% CrI: days 186–197) (Figure 3A). This suggests that, around the seasonal peak, tiger sharks that could be seen at the surface arrived and left at a fairly steady rate during our surveys. The smooth curve through the days of the year explained a small to moderate share of the variation in tiger shark sightings. Here Rm was 0.127 (95% CrI: 0.021–0.341) and Rc was 0.135 (95% CrI: 0.054–0.239).

The peak in tiger shark sightings came 28 days before the peak in fledgling numbers. The median shark sighting came 17 days before the median fledgling count. This shows that the sharks were most common before most fledglings were available to be eaten (Figure 3C). Shark sightings were already falling before fledgling numbers reached their seasonal highest point.

### 3.3. What in the Environment Might Drive the Seasonal Patterns (Aim 2)

To find which conditions mattered most, we used a machine-learning method called boosted regression trees (BRT). It builds many simple decision rules, one after another, to predict a number. We ran 1000 versions of each model, each built from a different random resample of our data (a method called bootstrapping). For each condition, the model gives a relative influence score, which shows how much that condition helped its predictions.

For tiger shark sightings, wind direction was the most important condition, with a relative influence of 27.3%. Next came the day of the year (20.6%), air pressure (12.5%) and air temperature (9.9%) (Figure 4). However, we were very uncertain about how much each condition really mattered, and the other conditions added relatively little to the model's predictions.

For fledgling numbers in the lagoon, the most important conditions were wind direction (23.4%), the day of the year (18.0%) and tide height (17.3%) (Figure 4). The other eight conditions added less to the model, and six of them scored below 9.1%.

FIGURE 4

Relative influence of environmental and timing conditions on tiger shark sightings and albatross fledgling numbers, based on 1000 bootstrapped boosted regression tree (BRT) models. Vertical dashed lines mark the cut-off between conditions that mattered and those that added less than expected background variation. Gray points and 95% confidence intervals show conditions below the cut-off, and green points and confidence intervals show conditions above it. (Tiger sharks) Conditions used to predict tiger shark counts, including wind direction, day of the year, air pressure and other environmental conditions. (Fledglings) Conditions used to predict albatross fledgling counts, including wind direction, day of the year, tide height and other environmental conditions.

The BRT models pointed to several conditions that helped their predictions a lot. But our second kind of model, the Bayesian generalized linear mixed model (GLMM), gave weak support for strong effects of these conditions on fledgling numbers and tiger shark sightings. This is likely because the two kinds of model do different jobs. BRT models focus on making good predictions. GLMMs test how strong a relationship is and how uncertain that estimate is in this particular place.

In the Bayesian GLMMs, the conditions that the BRT models found most important showed only weak links with tiger shark sightings. Wind direction (Figure 5A) and air pressure (Figure 5B) made little difference to the predicted effect on tiger shark sightings across the range of values we observed. The marginal R² showed that the main environmental factors explained very little of the variation in shark sightings (Rm = 0.029, 95% CI: 0.001–0.152). The conditional R² was higher (Rc = 0.38, 95% CI: 0.161–0.595). This means that more of the variation was linked to the timing of the season, captured by the random effects for the day of the year and the time of day.

The fledglings showed a similar picture. Wind direction (Figure 5C) and tide height (Figure 5D) made very little difference to the estimated number of fledglings across the range of values we observed. The marginal R² showed that the main environmental factors explained almost none of the variation in fledgling numbers (Rm = 0.009, 95% confidence interval (CI): 0.000–0.050). The conditional R² was much higher (Rc = 0.775, 95% CI: 0.699–0.840). This highlights the strong role of timing, captured by the random effects for the day of the year and the time of day.

FIGURE 5

How environmental conditions affected tiger shark counts (A, B) and albatross fledgling numbers (C, D), according to the Bayesian GLMMs. Gray points and lines show draws from the model's posterior distributions, which are the many possible values the model considers after seeing the data. Red points and trend lines show the estimated average effect.

### 3.4. How Often Sharks Caught Birds, and How the Meetings Unfolded (Aim 3)

During our observations over the fledging season, we recorded 26 meetings between tiger sharks and albatross fledglings. In 20 of these meetings (76.9%), the shark ended up eating the bird (Table 6 and Figure 6).

These 20 meetings mean that 1.3% of the fledglings we counted in the survey area over the season (1568 birds) were eaten. In most meetings, the shark rarely caught the bird on the first try. It had to approach again and again before it either succeeded or failed. Across all meetings, the shark made contact with the bird only 32.8% of the time (Figure 7).

### 3.5. How the Risk of Being Eaten Changed Through the Season (Aim 4)

The seasonal changes in predation seem to come mainly from when the prey and the predator were in the water at the same time, rather than from changes in how the sharks struck (Figure 8). Our model of the chance of a strike matched the patterns of fledglings and sharks over time. The chance of seeing a shark peaked earlier, on day 189 (95% CI: days 171–200), than the chance of seeing fledglings, which peaked on day 216 (95% CI: days 201–221).

The overall chance of a strike combines three things: whether fledglings were available, whether sharks were present, and the chance of a strike once both were there. It is found by multiplying these together. This overall chance peaked at about day 193 (95% CI: days 178–217). That is shortly after the peak in shark presence and about 3 weeks before fledglings were most available.

FIGURE 8

(B) Predicted chance of seeing tiger sharks during a survey. (C) Predicted chance of a tiger shark strike, given that both predator and prey are present. (D) Overall predicted chance of a tiger shark strike, combining predator presence, prey presence and the chance of a strike when both are present. Points show whether each survey saw the birds (1) or not (0). Lines show the middle (median) of the model's predictions, and shaded bands show the 95% credible intervals. Red dashed vertical lines mark the peak predicted chance, and gray boxes show the matching 95% credible intervals. Solid navy vertical lines mark the start and end of the period when tiger sharks were confirmed to be present.

The picture was different when we looked only at the chance of a strike once both fledglings and sharks were present. This chance showed no clear single peak over time (Figure 8C). It stayed broadly similar across the season. There was only a weak sign that it fell early in the season and then rose slightly after about day 200. Our uncertainty grew at the edges of the season, on days when there were few or no sharks and few meetings were recorded.
parts.discussion:
## 4. Discussion

In this study, we watched and counted tiger sharks eating fledglings directly, again and again, during a predictable burst of food. This gives a rare, measured view of how predators and prey interact. We know exactly when we saw sharks, when fledgling numbers were highest, and the middle (median) values of both. We also have clues about what might explain these patterns, how often the sharks caught birds, and how the chance of a shark catching a bird changed through the season.

### 4.1 Seasonal Timing of Tiger Shark Sightings and Fledgling Counts (Aim 1)

We expected shark sightings in the lagoon to rise and fall with the number of fledglings. Instead, we found a clear gap in time between the two. Tiger shark sightings peaked nearly a month, 28 days, before fledgling numbers peaked. The median shark sighting also came earlier in the season. This mismatch suggests that the sharks do not arrive when there are the most birds. Instead, they arrive while fledglings are just starting to appear in the lagoon.

This early-season overlap may be a time when fledglings are more vulnerable. Early in the fledging season, young birds that first enter the water are inexperienced, so they are probably easier for sharks to catch (Rice and Kenyon 1962). Shark sightings also dropped while fledgling numbers were still rising, which further supports this idea. It also fits with studies that tracked how some individual tiger sharks move during bursts of food, including albatross fledging in the Hawaiian chain (Meyer et al. 2010) and turtle nesting in the western Pacific (Fitzpatrick et al. 2012). Rather than staying for the whole burst of food, sharks may prefer to hunt when prey is easier to catch, rather than when prey is most plentiful and harder to catch.

This gap shows that the predator–prey relationship here follows a timing pattern, but the two are not in step. As a result, the risk of being eaten may be bunched up more than expected during the first stages of fledging. That is when sharks and fledglings are in the same place, with more sharks around and relatively few birds.

We should also see tiger sharks at Kure Atoll as part of the bigger picture of how tiger sharks move around the Northwestern Hawaiian Islands. Studies that tracked sharks with electronic tags have shown that tiger sharks can travel widely between islands in this region, including trips that involve Kure Atoll (Papastamatiou et al. 2013). At French Frigate Shoals, tiger sharks have been seen gathering with seasonal bursts of albatross fledglings. However, those tag studies also show that some sharks stay in these waters all year round (Lowe et al. 2006; Meyer et al. 2010; Papastamatiou et al. 2013; Blandino et al. 2025). The seasonal pattern we saw in sharks visible at the surface may show sharks arriving in and leaving the lagoon. This idea is supported by computer models and by what people who know the study area have observed.

### 4.2 What in the Environment Drives the Seasonal Patterns (Aim 2)

Environmental conditions had fairly weak links with the numbers of tiger sharks and fledglings we saw. Most of the ups and downs came from time of year instead. We used two kinds of statistical models. The first kind, called boosted regression trees (BRTs), picks out which conditions best help predict the counts. The second kind, called Bayesian generalized linear mixed models (Bayesian GLMMs), tests how strongly each condition is linked to the counts while allowing for the fact that some measurements are grouped together. The BRTs pointed to several conditions that seemed to matter a lot, but the Bayesian GLMMs did not strongly support these effects.

There was another problem. Several environmental conditions rose and fell in step with the day of the year (counted from the start of the season, called Julian day). This made it hard to tell their effects apart from the effect of time. Several conditions, including tide height and air pressure, followed repeating cycles, both over the 24-hour day and over the fledging season. So the time-based measures may have picked up wider seasonal changes in the system, which limited our ability to separate out the effects of each environmental condition on its own.

Wind direction had the strongest influence in the tiger shark BRT model. However, this link should be read with care. BRTs show which conditions help a model predict the counts, but they do not show that one thing causes another. The Bayesian GLMM gave little evidence that wind direction had a strong effect on how many tiger sharks we saw. So we do not treat wind direction as a direct or indirect cause of tiger sharks being in the study area.

The number of fledglings in the lagoon is probably driven by the natural timing of how the birds develop and when they fledge (Rice and Kenyon 1962; Sprague and Breuner 2010), rather than by short-term changes in the environment. In the same way, tiger shark sightings seem not to be linked to environmental conditions. Instead, they seem to be linked to how predictable a feeding area is (Holland et al. 1999; Heithaus et al. 2007; Meyer et al. 2009), including the seasonal burst of food that albatross fledglings provide (Lowe et al. 2006; Meyer et al. 2010).

The weak effects of the environmental conditions we tested in Aim 2 support the idea that the timing pattern found in Aim 1 is probably the main driver of both tiger shark sightings and fledgling numbers in this system.

### 4.3 How Often Sharks Caught Birds, and How the Meetings Unfolded (Aim 3)

Tiger sharks rarely caught fledglings on the first try, but they were very successful overall. Across all the meetings we watched, a shark caught a bird on its first strike only 32.8% of the time. Often, a shark had to try several times before it caught a bird. Only 19.2% of meetings (5 of 26) ended with the bird being eaten on the first strike. This shows that most successful catches took repeated attack attempts.

Even though first strikes rarely worked, once a meeting had started, the shark was very likely to succeed. Of the 26 meetings we watched, 76.9% (20 meetings) ended with the bird being eaten. This suggests that many fledglings are killed, even though the sharks and birds do not meet often. The difference between a low success rate on the first strike and a high success rate overall suggests that persistence, or keeping at it, is a key part of hunting success here.

Other studies have also found failed first attacks. Heithaus (2006) reported that dolphins often had bite scars from tiger sharks. This shows that failed attacks are common, with an estimated 11%–13% of dolphins in Shark Bay, Western Australia, attacked by sharks without being eaten. Observations of how tiger sharks hunt also suggest that they rely on sneaking up and taking chances, rather than spotting prey early, chasing at high speed, or situations that need quick, agile turns. These approaches lower the shark's chances of success (Heithaus et al. 2002). Our results fit with these findings, since repeated attack attempts made a catch more likely.

Tiger sharks may gain from meeting fledglings early in their development, when the birds still have a lot of downy feathers and cannot fly well (Rice and Kenyon 1962). This makes it harder for fledglings to get out of the water quickly after a failed attack. Under these conditions, repeated attack attempts make it more likely that the shark will eventually catch the bird.

The timing mismatch found in Aim 1 suggests that tiger sharks meet fledglings early in their development, when the birds cannot fly well. This may help explain why sharks were so successful once a meeting had started. Across the whole colony, few fledglings were killed by sharks: 1.3% of the fledglings we saw. This suggests that tiger sharks alone are unlikely to change the size of the colony much. However, because we surveyed three times a day, this estimate is probably too low.

Even so, the importance of this relationship for the ecosystem may not show up only in how many birds are killed. The overlap in time between tiger sharks and newly fledged albatrosses creates a period when the two are more likely to meet.

Tiger sharks may create a time of higher risk for fledglings after they enter the lagoon. But this risk is unlikely to change when fledglings fledge or where they spend their time. Fledglings must move into the ocean to learn to find food on their own, and the timing of fledging depends mainly on whether the birds are ready to develop (Rice and Kenyon 1962). So the presence of tiger sharks probably does not act as a signal that tells fledglings to enter the water. Instead, any higher risk of being eaten early in fledging probably reflects how poorly recently fledged birds can fly and escape once they meet a tiger shark in the lagoon.

### 4.4 How the Chance of Being Eaten Changed Through the Season (Aim 4)

The risk of being eaten changed mainly because of the seasonal overlap between tiger sharks and fledglings. It did not change because the sharks' striking behavior changed, or because the chance of an attack changed over time once a shark and a fledgling met. The overall chance of a strike was highest early in the fledging season, shortly after shark sightings peaked and before fledgling numbers peaked. This shows that the risk of being eaten is highest when predators and vulnerable prey are in the same place (Carrier et al. 2010).

In contrast, the chance of a strike once both sharks and fledglings were present showed no strong pattern over time and stayed fairly steady through the season. This suggests that the seasonal changes in risk did not come from changes in how likely the sharks were to attack. Instead, they came from changes in how likely sharks and prey were to be in the same place (Heithaus and Dill 2006). Early in the season, more tiger sharks were seen while fewer fledglings were available. Later in the season, fewer sharks were seen while fledgling numbers rose. So the changes in the chance of a strike seem to be shaped by when predators and prey are around, rather than by changes in the sharks' behavior once they meet. Tiger sharks are generalist hunters that take whatever chances come up (Ferreira et al. 2017). The risk to their prey depends on when the two are in the same place.

The model of the chance of a strike did show small changes over time, but there was no clear peak or pattern. We also had less certainty near the start and end of the season, when there were no sharks seen and few meetings happened. Together with the lack of a clear peak in catches, this may mean that rare strike events limited how well the model could detect patterns. So we treated the model's predictions in these parts of the season with care.

### 4.5 Limitations

Watching animals directly has several limits, and we kept them in mind when interpreting our results. We may have undercounted tiger shark sightings and fledglings because of things that block the view, such as glare from the sun, reflections from clouds, and waves on the lagoon's surface. Also, lightning stopped six surveys, which left small gaps in our coverage over time. One observer used the same survey method every time, which kept differences in effort and detection to a minimum. Even so, these factors may have added some bias to what we saw.

We studied only one fledging season at one place. So our study does not show how predator–prey relationships differ from year to year or from place to place. The 26 meetings we recorded are direct observations of how predators and prey interact during the fledging season at Kure Atoll. They give a measured starting point for studying predator–prey relationships during future fledging seasons at this and other places. More years of monitoring, done in the same standard way, would be valuable. It would show how steady the seasonal overlap between predators and prey, and the patterns of catching, are as environmental conditions and the amount of prey change from year to year.

The shark sightings we used could also be a source of uncertainty. We only surveyed the part of the lagoon that could be seen from the Green Island viewing point. This did not cover all of Kure Atoll, or all the places where tiger sharks might be. Also, if we did not see tiger sharks during a survey, that does not mean there were no sharks at Kure Atoll. They may have been outside the survey area, too deep below the surface to see, or active outside our survey times. Surveying during three standard daylight periods let us account for differences between survey times, but it did not show how tiger sharks use the area over the full 24-hour day. So the models that use our shark sightings probably underestimate how many sharks there really are. They should be read as showing the tiger sharks we saw at the surface within the survey area, not the true number of tiger sharks or whether sharks were present across the whole atoll.

Finally, our study focused mainly on what drives sightings and the risk of being eaten over time. But environmental conditions may still affect behavior and vulnerability in finer detail. Wind speed, for example, may help fledglings make quick escape moves (Udyawer et al. 2013; Weltz et al. 2013). Tide height (Schalff et al. 2014), how clear the water is, and glare may also play important roles in whether sharks manage to catch birds. Future studies that include these conditions, using more data, would help show how much behavior, the environment, and the animals' senses each shape whether a shark catches its prey.

### 4.6 What This Means More Widely

These results add to what we know about how predators and prey interact in nature. They also show something about how scientists use relationships worked out from indirect clues to predict what happens in nature. In the ocean in particular, studies of what animals eat (DeCrosta 1981; Stevens et al. 2000), studies that estimate fish populations (Hutchings and Myer 1994; Myers et al. 1996), and computer models of whole ecosystems (Grubbs et al. 2016) have been used in place of direct observations to measure predator–prey relationships. These approaches are valuable, but their results can strongly shape how people understand and manage nature when their assumptions are not tested.

Earlier work shows how much models of ecological patterns can shape decisions about managing nature. For example, models of trophic cascades and models of fish populations helped shape how people understood the collapse of Atlantic cod. A trophic cascade is a chain reaction in which a change in one part of a food web spreads to other levels. These models helped explain how the ecosystem was being reshaped and how fisheries were declining (Hutchings and Myer 1994; Myers et al. 1996). In a similar way, the public campaign "Save the Bay, Eat a Ray" grew out of the idea that fewer large sharks meant fewer cownose rays were being eaten, so the rays ate more shellfish. However, this trophic cascade idea was later challenged, because there was little evidence to support it and the assumptions about how the ecosystem works were uncertain (Grubbs et al. 2016).

In many uses of models, the results can depend on how uncertain the model's settings are, on the assumptions built into how the model is put together, and on how well it captures the real processes. This can lead to misleading predictions that can have serious effects on policy (Getz et al. 2018). One key study of trophic cascades in the ocean suggested that removing tiger sharks may reshape ocean food webs through indirect effects across several levels. It proposed that this would happen by increasing a middle-level consumer (seabirds), and that it could have devastating effects on lower levels of the food web (tuna) (Stevens et al. 2000). These model ideas were partly based on a snapshot in time of what 27 tiger sharks had eaten, found by examining their stomach contents (DeCrosta 1981). That study suggested that tiger sharks are key predators of fledglings.

With this in mind, direct observations collected over the time spans that matter in nature can help set the values in models and make them more reliable. Direct observations of predators and prey are especially useful for checking assumptions that would otherwise come from indirect methods. Our study shows that tiger sharks may have only a limited effect on how many fledglings die each year. This suggests that ecological models may need to be updated with these measured data on tiger shark behavior, which would lead to more accurate predictions of what happens in nature.

Our study also shows the value of keeping ecosystems fairly untouched by people, so that we can understand how nature works. Few places in the world have recorded tiger sharks gathering with seasonal bursts of prey (Fitzpatrick et al. 2012; Meyer et al. 2010). This makes the predator–prey relationships we watched directly at Kure Atoll a rare natural event of considerable importance. Protecting the Papahānaumokuākea Marine National Sanctuary, including its islands and its irreplaceable living laboratories, therefore protects not only species that need conservation. It also protects the chance to study long-standing relationships between living things that may have lasted across evolutionary and ecological time.

In conclusion, our study shows how much the vulnerability of prey, and when prey are available, shape predator–prey relationships during predictable bursts of food. The traditional idea is that the number of prey decides where predators are and how risky it is to be eaten. Our results show that predators may instead respond to the times when prey are easiest to catch. Tiger shark sightings in the lagoon came before fledgling numbers peaked, which shows that the sharks were most common in the survey area before the prey were most plentiful. Fledglings faced the highest rate of being eaten at the start of the fledging season, when inexperienced fledglings were probably most vulnerable. In fact, tiger shark sightings rose and then fell before fledgling numbers peaked. Our findings show that changes over time in how vulnerable and easy to reach prey are may matter more than how many prey there are in shaping predator behavior.

More broadly, our study is one of the few works that looks at how large ocean predators hunt during predictable, short bursts of food. Few places in the world report tiger sharks gathering with seasonal bursts of prey (Fitzpatrick et al. 2012; Meyer et al. 2010), and none have directly measured how the timing of predators, prey vulnerability, and catching success are linked. By recording these behaviors across a whole fledging season, our findings show how predators' responses to prey conditions that change over time can create patterns in the risk of being eaten. Our study suggests that changes over time in how vulnerable prey are are an important way that predator behavior connects to patterns in nature during systems with bursts of food.
